book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature

chapters.file: ch16 - The Fall of the House of Ulmer Europe vs. America in the Gothic Vision of The Black Cat.md
chapters.relation: Cantor reads Edgar Ulmer's The Black Cat (1934) as a European emigre's Gothic allegory of Europe vs. America, with Karloff's architect Poelzig and Lugosi's psychiatrist Werdegast as mirror-image 'living dead' fixated on the horrors of World War I. He connects Poelzig's modernist house-over-Fort-Marmaros to a Freudian map of ego and id and to the war-driven rise of psychoanalysis, and reads the naive, unconscious American honeymooners against the cultured but nihilistic Europeans. He explicitly links the film's high-culture/pop-culture opposition to Heidegger's vision of Europe squeezed between a leveling America and Russia and to the Frankfurt School critique of American mass entertainment.

chapters.file: ch17 - From Domestic Nightmares to the Nightmare of History Uncanny Eruptions of Violence in King's and Kubrick's Ver.md
chapters.relation: Lutz argues that King's novel and Kubrick's film of The Shining both stage Freud's uncanny as the return of a repressed, corporeal past: the woman in Room 217 and Grady's ghosts, the father-mirroring of Jack, his abusive father, and Delbert Grady, and Danny's Tony double. He reads King as an 'inverted family romance' where the good replacement father is the Black cook Hallorann, then shows Kubrick widening domestic abuse into a Marxian nightmare of history: the Overlook built on an Indian burial ground, the Calumet cans, and Jack's craving to join the hotel's ghostly 'management' expose the racist, patriarchal, class violence founding American institutions. Jack's 'All work and no play' manuscript figures his entrapment in ideology and repetition.

chapters.file: ch18 - “Hot with Rapture and Cold with Fear” Grotesque, Sublime, and Postmodern Transformations in Patrick Süskind's.md
chapters.relation: Cokal reads Suskind's Perfume and Tykwer's film through the intertwined categories of the grotesque and the sublime. The odorless murderer Grenouille is a Bakhtinian grotesque body who nonetheless has Kantian sublime experiences of the plum girl's and Laure's scents, and Cokal uses Kant's and Lyotard's accounts of the sublime (the soul 'immobilized, as good as dead') to explain the awe that Grenouille both feels and, via his 'angel's scent,' induces in the orgy at his execution. Grenouille's uncanny encounter with his own lack of smell in the cave is read through Freud's uncanny, and his final cannibalistic dismemberment collapses the sublime back into the grotesque.

chapters.file: ch19 - Shock Value A Deleuzean Encounter with James Purdy's Narrow Rooms.md
chapters.relation: Gross stages a Deleuze-and-Guattari 'encounter' with Purdy's Narrow Rooms, refusing Freudian or Marxist 'interpretosis' in favor of asking what the novel does. He reads Roy Sturtevant the 'renderer' as a multiplicity and traces the characters' becomings-animal (Sid's 'becoming-shark' in the locker-room sex act, becoming-horse, becoming-insect) and the crucifixion of Roy on the barn door as horror that dissolves the boundaries between master and slave, lover and torturer. Invoking Deleuze's debt to Spinoza, Nietzsche, and the Stoics, Gross argues that the joyful amor fati of art embraces horror as an expansion of life rather than something to be vanquished.

chapters.file: ch20 - Making Monsters The Philosophy of Reproduction in Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Universal Films Frankens.md
chapters.relation: Hall reads Shelley's Frankenstein and the 1931 film and its 1935 Bride sequel through Luce Irigaray's Speculum, arguing that Victor's and Walton's quests for a whole, self-sufficient identity enact a patriarchal desire to reproduce sameness and deny the 'maternal waters,' with women reduced to mirrors that will not reflect. She uses Lacan's mirror stage and the camera's power over sight to explain how identity is fixed by being seen, and Derrida's 'Structure, Sign and Play' to recast identity as a perpetually rewritten, misshapen text. The Bride's refusing scream and the exploding phallic tower mark female desire as a negating power that disrupts patriarchal reproduction.

chapters.file: ch21 - Kitsch and Camp and Things That Go Bump in the Night; or, Sontag and Adorno at the (Horror) Movies.md
chapters.relation: Johnston uses his childhood TV horror host Sir Graves Ghastly to distinguish kitsch from camp in the horror genre. Drawing on Greenberg's 'Avant-garde and Kitsch' and Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, he argues that the Universal Horror sequels, Jaws, and most slasher films are kitsch: nonchallenging, formulaic variations that pacify consumers, while autonomous works like Carpenter's They Live or Craven's Scream interrogate the genre. Via Sontag's 'Notes on Camp' and Isherwood's making-fun-of versus making-fun-out-of, he sorts They Live, Scream, I Know What You Did Last Summer, and Scary Movie into deliberate camp, naive camp, and mere kitsch.

holes.name: Becoming and Deterritorialization
holes.what: Deleuze and Guattari's account of 'becoming' (becoming-animal, becoming-imperceptible) and lines of flight that dissolve fixed molar identities into molecular multiplicities.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire Deleuzean reading turns on becoming-shark, multiplicity, and lines of flight, which the taxonomy's only Deleuze slug (rhizome) does not adequately capture.

holes.name: Luce Irigaray
holes.what: French feminist philosopher and psychoanalyst whose Speculum of the Other Woman critiques the phallocentric, mirror-logic of Western philosophy and theorizes feminine multiplicity ('two lips').
holes.why: Chapter 20's reading of Frankenstein and reproduction is structured throughout by Irigaray's Speculum, but she has no slug in the taxonomy's philosopher list.

holes.name: Camp (Sontag's sensibility)
holes.what: Susan Sontag's aesthetic 'sensibility' that prizes artifice, exaggeration, theatricality and 'the good taste of bad taste,' seeing the world as Being-as-Playing-a-Role.
holes.why: Chapter 21's central argument sorts horror films by the camp sensibility from Sontag's 'Notes on Camp,' a concept the taxonomy has no adequate slug for (culture-industry covers only the Adorno/kitsch side).
